title: Data Wrangling using R and Introduction to GIS applications using ArcPro
text:
This course provides foundational skills in data science and Geographic Information Systems (GIS). It is divided into two main sections:

data processing, visualization, and R programming using the tidyverse, and
an introduction to GIS using ESRI’s ArcPro software.






The goal of this section is to give students a broad understanding of data processing, visualization, in the R programming environment. Students will investigate a range of features in the tidyverse package over the course in order to assemble a toolkit for effective data wrangling and visualization.



This section is designed to provide students with a practical introduction to Geographic Information Systems (GIS) using ESRI’s ArcPro software. The section will focus on building foundational GIS skills and understanding its practical applications. Each week will introduce new concepts and will cover specific ArcPro tools to enhance hands-on learning.






Meeting Time: 4 hours of combined lecture and lab per week.

Each class will be roughly divided into two sections:

Data wrangling, visualization, and programming, and
Building GIS skills using ArcPro.

A short lecture for each section will introduce the week’s concepts, and then students will complete in-class exercises.




Your final grade will be based on the following components:

Class Participation: 20%
Project 1: R & Data Visualization: 40%

Create an R Markdown or Quarto document and serve it as a standalone website (using GitHub pages) showing data wrangling and visualization skills. You can provide your own data from your thesis project or I can help you find a dataset (likely NCRMP related).

Project 2: GIS Mapping: 40%

Create GIS map(s) in ArcGIS Pro visualizing your data. Again, you can use your own data or NCRMP-related data.







R: The R programming language, available from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN).
RStudio: The RStudio Desktop IDE, available from the Posit website.
ArcGIS Pro: ESRI’s desktop GIS software. Licensing and download information will be provided.
Git: A version control system. Please download and install it from the official Git website.
GitHub: A web-based platform for version control. You will need to create a free account.

title: Appendix
text:
This appendix provides a quick reference for functions and tools covered in class.

R FunctionsArcPro Tools






Description: Returns the class or type of an R object.
Example: class(my_variable)






Description: Displays the internal structure of an R object.
Example: str(iris)






Description: A dplyr function that provides a transposed view of str().
Example: glimpse(iris)






Description: A readr function for reading .csv files.
Example: read_csv("my_data.csv")






Description: A readxl function for reading Excel files.
Example: read_xlsx("my_data.xlsx")






Description: A writexl function for writing to an .xlsx file.
Example: write_xlsx(my_dataframe, "output.xlsx")






Description: A base R function for selecting rows and columns.
Example: subset(iris, Species == "setosa")






Description: A dplyr function to select rows based on their values.
Example: filter(iris, Sepal.Length > 7)






Description: A dplyr function to select columns by name.
Example: select(iris, Petal.Length, Petal.Width)






Description: The pipe operator from magrittr that chains operations together.
Example: iris %>% filter(Species == "versicolor") %>% select(Petal.Width)






Description: Used to create conditions for filtering. Includes ==, !=, >, <, & (AND), | (OR).
Example: filter(iris, Species == "setosa" & Petal.Width > 0.2)






Description: A dplyr function that returns all rows from the left table (x), and all columns from both x and y.
Example: left_join(table1, table2, by = "common_column")






Description: A dplyr function that returns all rows from the right table (y), and all columns from both x and y.
Example: right_join(table1, table2, by = "common_column")






Description: A dplyr function that returns all rows and all columns from both tables.
Example: full_join(table1, table2, by = "common_column")






Description: A dplyr function that returns only the rows from both tables that have matching values.
Example: inner_join(table1, table2, by = "common_column")






Description: A dplyr function that adds new variables or transforms existing ones.
Example: mutate(iris, Petal.Area = Petal.Length * Petal.Width)






Description: A dplyr function that collapses a data frame to a single row with summary statistics.
Example: summarize(iris, avg_sepal_length = mean(Sepal.Length))






Description: A dplyr function for applying multiple if/else conditions.
Example: mutate(iris, size = case_when(Sepal.Length > 5 ~ "big", TRUE ~ "small"))






Description: A dplyr function used to group a data frame by one or more variables.
Example: iris %>% group_by(Species) %>% summarize(avg_petal_length = mean(Petal.Length))






Description: A tidyr function that “lengthens” data, increasing the number of rows and decreasing the number of columns.
Example: data %>% pivot_longer(cols = c(col1, col2), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")






Description: A tidyr function that “widens” data, increasing the number of columns and decreasing the number of rows.
Example: data %>% pivot_wider(names_from = "variable", values_from = "value")






Description: A tidyr function that splits a single character column into multiple columns.
Example: data %>% separate(col = "combined_col", into = c("new_col1", "new_col2"), sep = "-")






Description: A tidyr function that combines multiple columns into a single character column.
Example: data %>% unite("new_combined_col", col1, col2, sep = "_")






Description: Executes a block of code repeatedly for each item in a sequence.
Example:
for (i in 1:5) {
  print(paste("This is loop number", i))
}






Description: Controls the flow of code execution based on logical conditions.
Example:
x <- 10
if (x > 20) {
  print("x is large")
} else if (x > 5) {
  print("x is medium")
} else {
  print("x is small")
}






Description: Creates a new, reusable function to perform a specific task.
Example:
add_numbers <- function(a, b) {
  return(a + b)
}






Description: A tidyr function that creates a list-column containing data frames. It’s a cornerstone of working with nested data.
Example: data %>% group_by(group_var) %>% nest()






Description: A function from the purrr package that applies a function to each element of a list or vector, returning a list. It’s an alternative to for loops for iterative operations.
Example: nested_data %>% mutate(model = map(data, ~lm(y ~ x, data = .)))






Description: A function from the broom package that takes the messy output of a model and turns it into a tidy data frame.
Example: model %>% tidy()





Description: A function to standardize and clean column names of data frames.
Example: model %>% clean_names()





Description: A function to convert a string to all lowercase.
Example: str_to_lower("Make_alL_oF_ThIS_lower_CASE")





Description: A function to extract the first number found within a string, ignoring any non-numeric characters before or after it.
Example: parse_number("extract_only_the_25")








Description: Aggregates features based on specified attributes.






Description: Converts Microsoft Excel files into a table in your geodatabase.






Description: Creates a new point feature class based on x- and y-coordinates in a table.






Description: Calculates the values of a field for a feature class or table.






Description: Extracts input features that overlay the clip features. Like using a cookie cutter.






Description: Creates buffer polygons around input features to a specified distance.






Description: Extracts the cell values of a raster based on a set of point features.






Description: Creates a shaded relief raster from a digital elevation model (DEM).






Description: The process of assigning visual variables to map features to convey information.






Description: Combines multiple input datasets of the same data type into a single, new output dataset.






Description: Adds features from one or more datasets into an existing target dataset.






Description: Computes a geometric intersection of input features. Only the overlapping features are written to the output.






Description: Joins attributes from one feature to another based on their spatial relationship.






Description: Extracts the cells of a raster that correspond to the areas defined by a mask.






Description: Summarizes the values of a raster within the zones of another dataset.






Description: Creates a feature class containing points generated from the representative locations of input features.






Description: Calculates the area of each feature from one layer that falls within the classes of another raster layer.






Description: Calculates the rate of change in elevation for each cell of a raster.






Description: Identifies the downslope direction of the maximum rate of change in value from each cell to its neighbors.






Description: Creates a line feature class of contours (isolines) from a raster surface.






Description: Converts a raster dataset to a polygon feature class.






Description: Builds and executes a single Map Algebra expression using a Python syntax.






Description: A collection of tools and workflows for creating new vector features and modifying existing ones.






Description: Creates a feature class containing polygons or polylines which represent a specified minimum bounding geometry.






Description: Creates a net of rectangular cells (a fishnet).






Description: A suite of tools (like IDW, Kriging, Spline) used to estimate values at unsampled locations.






Description: A visual programming language for building geoprocessing workflows.






Description: A set of tools used to align raster or vector data to a known coordinate system. This is often done by creating control points that link locations in the data to known real-world coordinates.

title: GIS Data Organization
text:
Before you map your first reef or run a single spatial analysis, you must establish a system for organizing your data.
In marine ecology, you will deal with massive raster datasets (like sea surface temperature or bathymetry) alongside specific field data (like transect surveys or benthic cover classifications). Without a deliberate storage strategy, your project will quickly become a tangled web of broken links, duplicated multi-gigabyte files, and lost analysis steps right before your thesis defense.
This guide covers how to set up your files, distinguish between project-specific data and master reference data on your computer, and maintain clean spatial hygiene.

title: GIS Data Organization
section: 1. What ArcGIS Pro Sets Up Automatically
text:
1. What ArcGIS Pro Sets Up Automatically
When you create a new project using the “Map” template, ArcGIS Pro creates a directory for your project. Think of this folder as the physical container for your workspace.
Inside that directory, Pro automatically generates a very specific file structure:
Brewers_Bay_Project/   <-- The main project folder
│
├── Brewers_Bay_Project.aprx  # The Project File
├── Brewers_Bay_Project.gdb   # The Default Geodatabase
├── Brewers_Bay_Project.atbx  # The Default Toolbox (for your models/scripts)
├── ImportLog/                # Temporary workspace for imported documents
├── Index/                    # Search and metadata indexing files
└── .backups/                 # Automatic project save backups (hidden folder)

The .aprx file is NOT your data!
The .aprx file acts like a display window. It stores your map layouts, colors, and instructions on where to look for the data. No spatial coordinates, rasters, or data attributes live inside the .aprx file. If you email just the .aprx file to your advisor, they will see a map full of broken red exclamation marks.

title: GIS Data Organization
section: 2. Project-Specific Data vs. Personal “Shared” Reference Data
text:
2. Project-Specific Data vs. Personal “Shared” Reference Data
The biggest mistake is keeping all your data inside a single project folder, or dumping everything onto your Desktop.
To keep your laptop’s hard drive clean and avoid duplicating massive datasets, you need to mentally separate your data into two categories: Project-Specific and Reference.

A. The Reference Library (Shared Across All Your Projects)
You should create a single folder (e.g., C:/GIS/ReferenceData/) that acts as a central library for large, immutable datasets you will use repeatedly across different classes, chapters, or side projects. You should never edit or run tools that save outputs into this directory unless its necessary.
What belongs here?

Global or regional bathymetry (e.g., GEBCO, local LiDAR DEMs)
Climatologies (e.g., NOAA Coral Reef Watch Sea Surface Temperature rasters)
Global boundary files (e.g., Global Distribution of Coral Reefs UNEP dataset, EEZ boundaries, landmass polygons)
Unchanging basemaps or large satellite imagery mosaics

C:/GIS/ReferenceData/
│
├── Bathymetry/
│   ├── GEBCO_2026_Global_Grid.tif
│   └── Hawaii_LiDAR_Bathymetry_5m.tif
├── Oceanography/
│   └── NOAA_SST_Monthly_Climatology_2010_2020.gdb
└── Boundaries_and_Baselines/
    ├── UNEP_WCMC_Global_Coral_Reefs.shp
    └── US_Exclusive_Economic_Zones.gdb


B. The Project-Specific Geodatabase (ProjectName.gdb)
This is the .gdb created inside your specific project folder. It holds data unique to the specific research question or assignment you are working on right now. This will be automatically created for you when you start a new project in ArcPro. You should create a single folder to house all your projects (e.g., C:/GIS/Projects/Brewers_Bay_Project/)
What belongs here?

Intermediate scratch files: (e.g., a bathymetry layer clipped only to Brewers Bay)
Primary field data: (e.g., GPS points of coral colonies you sampled, imported from a CSV)
Geoprocessing outputs: (e.g., Buffer polygons around marine protected areas, hotspot analysis results)

title: GIS Data Organization
section: 3. The Recommended Workspace Layout and Putting It All Together
text:
3. The Recommended Workspace Layout and Putting It All Together
A well organized project looks like this on your computer. Notice how it references the Reference Library but keeps local operations safely contained:
C:/GIS/Projects/Brewers_Bay_Project/
│
├── Brewers_Bay_Project.aprx        # The map document
├── Brewers_Bay_Project.gdb         # ALL output files and clipped data go here
│   ├── brewers_bathymetry_clip     # (Derived from your Reference folder)
│   ├── transect_points_2026        # (Imported from 01_RawData)
│   └── bleaching_hotspot_polygons  # (Final analysis output)
│
├── Brewers_Bay_Project.atbx
│
├── 01_Raw_Field_Data/                     
│   ├── benthic_survey_raw_2026.csv
│   ├── dive_gps_tracks.gpx
│   └── metadata_field_notes.txt
│
├── 02_Reference_Shortcuts/ # Optional: Read-only shortcuts to C:/GIS/ReferenceData/
│
└── 03_Final_Exports/ # Where you save outputs for your thesis/publications
    ├── Fig1_Brewers_Study_Site_300dpi.jpg
    ├── Fig2_Bleaching_Extent.pdf
    └── summary_statistics.csv

title: GIS Data Organization
text:
4. Conventions of GIS Data Hygiene

Keep Raw Data Raw: Never do spatial operations directly on your original field CSVs or master shapefiles. Always import them into your project .gdb first.
Name Like a Programmer: ArcGIS Pro hates spaces and special characters. Avoid names like Transects (Final) v2 - copy.shp. Use snake_case or CamelCase instead: brewers_transects_final_v2.
Always Check the Geoprocessing Output Path: Whenever you run a tool (like a Buffer or Clip), Pro will try to guess where to save the output. Always verify it is pointing to your Project .gdb, not your C:/GIS/Reference/ folder, and not the default temporary Scratch.gdb.
Think Before You Save: “Is this dataset only relevant to this bay on this specific day?” -> Project .gdb. “Will I need this continuous map of ocean depth for my next three projects?” -> Reference Folder.

title: GIS Data Organization in R
text:
Before you begin analysis in R, you must establish a system for organizing your files and directories.
You will often deal with large datasets (from colleagues or off the web) alongside specific field data (like fish transect counts or benthic quadrat surveys). Without a deliberate storage strategy, your workflow will quickly become overwhelming and confusing.
This guide covers how RStudio Projects work, how conventions will help you maintain project organization.

title: GIS Data Organization in R
text:
1. What RStudio Sets Up Automatically
When you create a new project in RStudio (File > New Project…), RStudio creates a self-contained directory anchored by an .Rproj file. Think of this folder as the physical container for your entire workspace.
Inside that directory, RStudio establishes a clean baseline layout:
Brewers_Bay_Ecology/            <-- The main project folder
│
├── Brewers_Bay_Ecology.Rproj   # The RStudio Project File
└── .Rproj.user/                # User-specific RStudio preferences (hidden)

Why standardizing with .Rproj matters
Opening an .Rproj file launches a fresh R session and automatically sets your working directory (getwd()) to the project root folder.
In traditional workflows, researchers often relied on setwd() with absolute paths (e.g., setwd(“C:/Users/name/Desktop/project”)). Using setwd() with absolute paths guarantees that code will break on anyone else’s computer—or even on your own machine if you move the folder.
RStudio Projects make your workflow portable: as long as all files live inside this directory, the whole folder can be moved, zipped, or shared via GitHub, and all relative file paths will continue to work seamlessly.

title: GIS Data Organization in R
text:
2. The Recommended Workspace Layout
A well-structured RStudio project is completely self-contained. Every file required to run your analysis, from raw field CSVs to processing scripts and rendered reports lives within sub directories of the root folder:
Brewers_Bay_Ecology/
│
├── Brewers_Bay_Ecology.Rproj    # RStudio project anchor
│
├── data/                        # Primary data directory
│   ├── raw/                     # Read-only field survey CSVs, raw GPS points
│   └── processed/               # processed data you generated from the raw.
│
├── outputs/                     # Generated deliverables
│   ├── figures/                 # Publication-ready map figures (.png, .pdf)
│   └── tables/                  # Exported summary statistics (.csv)
│
├── scripts/                     # Standalone .R scripts
│   ├── 01_data_cleaning.R
│   ├── 02_my_custom_functions.R
│   └── 03_spatial_analysis.R
│
└── docs/                        # Quarto (.qmd) files and rendered HTML/PDF reports
    └── index.qmd

title: GIS Data Organization in R
text:
3. Subdirectory Breakdown & Data Conventions

data/
This folder contains all source and derived data required for your analysis.

data/raw/: Stores your original datasets. Convention: Raw data files must be strictly read-only. Never edit, overwrite, or clean raw data files manually in Excel or R[cite: 2].
data/processed/: Holds cleaned, transformed, or derived datasets generated programmatically by your R scripts.



outputs/
This folder holds all deliverables generated by your R scripts.

Save generated figures (.png, .pdf) and statistical tables here.
Convention: Treat everything in outputs/ as disposable and fully reproducible. You should be able to delete the entire outputs/ folder, re-run your scripts, and regenerate every file automatically.



scripts/
This folder houses modular R code files (.R).

Separate your processing steps into distinct scripts rather than maintaining one massive, thousands-of-lines-long script.
Prefix script names with sequential numbers (e.g., 01_load_and_clean_data.R, 02_site_level_stats.R, 03_plot_site_level_data.R) so anyone opening the project knows the exact order in which to run them.



docs/
This folder is dedicated to Quarto documents (.qmd) and rendered output reports (.html, .pdf).

Isolating Quarto files and their rendered assets in docs/ keeps your root folder tidy and makes publishing reports via platforms like GitHub Pages straightforward.
